title: Salsa Blackthorn 125 Review: I’m Buying this Bike – Travis Engel
content:
The Salsa Blackthorn 125 is one of a growing number of moderate-travel bikes with immoderate geometry. But it’s also got a few tricks up its sleeve that are very Salsa, and evidently, very Travis.

I guess I spoiled it in the title, but this review is going to be pretty positive. That tends to happen when the bike I’m writing about was tailor-made for me and my mountains. The aggressive-125mm-rear-travel-140mm-front-travel-trail-bike category is very much my jam. And I would call it a category. The Esker Howdy, the Norco Optic, the Canyon Lux Trail (and the Spectral 125 that it replaced) are all in the same league. And all are in the top 10 bikes I’ve ridden this decade. I figured the Salsa Blackthorn 125 would be a shoe-in, but something left me a little doubtful.

Bike journalists often look over each other’s shoulders to learn about what’s trending and hear stories we might have missed. Pinkbike is usually my first stop as I sit down with my morning coffee. I’ve worked with a lot of the folks over there. They know their stuff, and I trust their opinions. And they were more than critical of the Blackthorn 125. They complained of harsh rear suspension, a low stack height, and short chainstays. But a western Canadian’s “harsh” may be a southern Californian’s “poppy,” even though they tested it in northern Arkansas. And stack heights can be fixed, and short chainstays can be fun. I had to see this thing for myself.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Quick Hits

  • 125mm rear travel, 140 front
  • Also available in 145 / 160 version, convertible by swapping shock, yoke, and fork internals
  • 29” wheels only
  • Carbon front and rear triangle
  • Aluminum version available
  • Split-pivot linkage design
  • Coil-shock compatible
  • Two full-sized in-triangle bottle cages on all frame sizes
  • Integrated accessory strap
  • 33.8 lbs (XL, with Lyrik fork* and without pedals)
  • $3,499 starting price with aluminum frame and Eagle 70 Transmission
  • $4,799 as tested*
    • *Stock builds run RockShox Pike Select, not Lyrik Select as pictured

Salsa’s suspension flip chips default to their “high” position. That’s not often the case these days, and it was the first thing I changed. That got me a slack-for-the-category 64.4° head-tube angle and retains a steep-for-any-category 77.9° seat tube angle. The Blackthorn’s reach numbers are nearly a full rung higher than today’s standard sizing ladders, but I still stuck with an XL with a 518mm reach. And the XL’s 635mm stack is indeed on the low side. It’s 10mm lower than an XL Specialized Epic XC race bike, though the Epic’s head tubes are a bit tall for the category. And maybe there’s a reason the Blackthorn kept it low.

Blackthorn 125 (left) and Blackthorn 145 (right)

There’s also another flavor Blackthorn, with 145mm of rear travel and 160 front. It uses the same frame, but a shorter shock mount, longer shock, and of course a longer fork. Stretching the Blackthorn’s head tube another inch may have been a bit much for that setup. A bar / stem upgrade isn’t an enormous expense, but I wish Salsa had specced a higher cockpit on the Blackthorn 125. Its built-in capability deserves a more downhill-friendly posture. After all, this is a downsized all-mountain bike, not an upsized XC bike. But true to the Salsa credo, it’s still an adventure bike.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Design Details

Two full-sized bottles! That’s at least 48 ounces of freedom! Sure, Salsa couldn’t quite get that ultra-low dirt-jumper silhouette, where the top tube leads straight into the seatstays. But who cares? Standover doesn’t matter until well past the front of the saddle nose, if it matters at all. There’s ample room for a 150mm dropper post on a size small, and probably more. I’m currently running a 220mm on my XL with room to spare. The storage space is worth the slightly bigger triangle. And then there’s that little triangle up front with an even littler strap mount.

Bottom three photos: Travis Engel

There’s nothing stopping you from strapping any object to any frame tube, whether or not that frame tube is designed for straps. But this mount does keep the strap in place while you’re handling that object. It’s a nice added convenience. It also just gets you thinking about what you could use it for. Same goes for the top-tube mount, which I still haven’t decided on. I did a couple rides with a snack bag, a couple rides with a double Wolf Tooth B-Rad strap system holding a handsaw, and I’m working out the kinks of some Fidlock accessories. I kinda wish Salsa had also added under-down-tube mounts. But again, nothing’s stopping you from strapping objects down there, either.

Cable routing is fully guided, including through the chainstays. I just swapped this bike’s brakes for a review, and I appreciated the ease of just pushing a hose in one end and seeing it come out the other. Also, kudos to Salsa for routing the derailleur housing through the top of the chainstay instead of the bottom, making for a smoother line and smoother shifting. And there are a few other little nice touches. Like, the forward shock eyelet runs directly on a thick hollow bolt, which is held in place with an expanding collet. There’s a little mud flap to keep debris from getting stuck behind the main pivot, and generous stay protection.

Then there’s Split Pivot. It’s a linkage-driven single-pivot where one of the pivots is concentric to the rear axle. With regards to pedaling and pumping, Split Pivot doesn’t do anything that any other design couldn’t. But it does eliminate the rear brake’s tendency to excessively compress the rear suspension. Split Pivot seems to have its supporters, with patens from both Dave Weagle and (in a legally distinct form) from Trek. But personally, I think Split Pivot is … fine. Brake interference just doesn’t annoy me on a ride. At least not in a way that I can pluck from the chaos and put into words. It stands out even less when the travel is this short and this supportive. Split Pivot didn’t make itself known for better or worse during my testing. But we’ve got more to talk about before I get to ride impressions.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Spec and Value

Increasingly, we’re seeing brands set a floor of $5,000, $6,000 or higher for their carbon full-suspension mountain bikes. And aluminum options are becoming more and more rare. With that in mind, I think the Blackthorn 125 lineup is pretty reasonably priced, especially for bikes you can buy from your brick-and-mortar shop. My $4,800 test bike’s frame, suspension, drivetrain, and wheels are solid. No notes aside from its ugly color. Even the WTB wheels surprised me. Their OEM-only models have been kinda clunky in the past, but I’d happily ride these until they die. My only complaint is the mid-powered SRAM DB6 brakes. They’re great as a budget option, but not if you’re trying to push a bike to its limits.

The $3,500 alloy version has similarly good bones, and I’m glad the metal fans weren’t given bottom-tier suspension or an outdated drivetrain. But the clear standout is the $4,000 carbon version specced with previous-generation Deore, though it’s out of stock and the folks at Salsa couldn’t yet share their plans for that tier’s future. In fact, inventory is spotty on all models at the time of publishing, But this iteration of the Blackthorn is barely a year and a half old, so stocks will be replenished. And hey, maybe your local shop has one on the shelf right now.

Test-Bike Setup

I made a couple significant changes within the first week of having the Blackthorn 125, and they deserve their own subheading. I always swap out a test bike’s handlebars for my Doom Lucky Risers because their 14° backsweep makes a new bike feel more like home. But I also added my Ergotec High Bass stem to boost their already generous 50mm rise. I did a lot of experimenting with headset spacers, and I ended up with the 20mm stack shown here. It looks odd, and only taller riders will want to go this extreme. But unless you’re looking for a race-like posture, I recommend raising the bar.

Photo: Travis Engel

While the cockpit change happened before I’d even aired up the tires, my shock adjustments happened over a few rides. The first such adjustment was to start removing volume spacers. My RockShox-equipped model came packed with the maximum of four Bottomless Tokens. Fox-equipped models are working on a different scale, but they come stock with a 0.6 and 0.1 cubic-inch reducer, which is still a lot. Of course, a brand giving you more reducers is better than fewer reducers. You can just take them out. I recommend anyone buying this model give that a try.

Photos: Travis Engel

In both its 125 and 145mm configurations, the Blackthorn’s linkage is designed to be progressive. It works with coil shocks, and the flagship 145 model uses Fox’s large-air-volume Float X2 shock. After removing three—then all four—of my test bike’s spacers, I eventually got RockShox to send their Linear XL air can upgrade kit ($105), which increases volume. The standard volume spacers still work, and the air can itself accommodates a few more if necessary. I spent most of my time with that Linear XL air can with two traditional volume spacers to reel it back in a tad. And now it’s probably time to finally talk about how it rides.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Ride Impressions: Climbing

With its initial shock-volume configuration, the Blackthorn’s rear end felt much like the Canyon Lux Trail I just reviewed. That is; like an XC bike. Peppy, but not plush. Even running just a hair under 30% sag, it felt more like a 100mm than 125. This wouldn’t be an unreasonable setup for heavier riders and / or riders who are especially allergic to bottom-outs. Even for me, it didn’t feel “wrong,” but it did feel like the shock could do a better job helping me out on the bumps without sacrificing much efficiency. The stock air can empty of volume spacers did just that. It allowed me to find a setup that bridged the gap between that XC pep and the cloudlike indifference I eventually teased out of the Esker Howdy.

That more supportive feeling suited the Blackthorn 125’s geometry well. The short chainstays help it respond quickly and precisely on punchy, technical climbs. And the steep seat-tube angle kept the front wheel reasonably well planted to the ground. I even slid my saddle back a little after we captured the beauty shots in this review. It feels quite natural on challenging climbs that demand high effort and high precision. When I had to twist around and over obstacles, it had a nearly trials-y responsiveness.

And the geometry is doing a lot of the work here. Again, there’s no hidden magic in how Split Pivot responds to pedaling force. The Esker Howdy’s Orion Link, the Revel Rascal’s CBF, and the Norco Optic’s high pivot all offered built-in flotation on rough, high-torque climbs. If you could keep your body weight steady, those bikes could remain stoically neutral in their travel. The Blackthorn isn’t the hoverbike they are. It favors support over suppleness, but that’s still a perfectly valid approach. Even after I switched to the Linear XL air can, I never got sucked into the late-stroke doldrums in the occasional frantic mash up a rocky shelf.

And on that note, I loved seeing a 30-tooth chainring. I hope that’ll become a trend in non-XC bikes. Beyond just giving a lower low end, it allowed me to stay in smaller cogs for longer for a straighter chainline. That ring also pairs well with the 165mm crank arms that all the kids run these days. Speaking of which, I can’t remember having a single harsh pedal strike on the Blackthorn 125. Even in the “low” setting, my feet stayed out of harm’s way. It was enough to make me wish Salsa had gone a little lower. It’d be a way to pad out the stack height and lean into the bike’s natural aptitudes on the descents, but let’s not get ahead of ourselves.

While very few bikes are bad at smooth climbs like fire roads and groomed singletrack, the Blackthorn 125 is decidedly good. That supportive suspension kept it from getting too floaty as I spun my legs, and I love a horizontally mounted shock for convenient access to the lockout. And the geometry helped here, too. This bike has the longest reach of any bike I’ve ever spent more than a minute on. It paired well with the steep seat-tube angle. I’ve long argued that the “cramped” seated cockpits of some modern trail and enduro bikes aren’t actually as inefficient as they’re made out to be. Sitting and spinning can be done while upright. But having my hands a half-inch farther forward did make high-torque efforts a little easier.

And let’s not forget the impact of all the on-bike storage. In the month I’ve been riding this bike, I haven’t carried water on my back once. That moved some mass farther forward where it couldn’t tug as hard on the rear shock. But it also moved it off my back, and by extension, off my saddle. Plus, it totally upends the packing paradigm. When your excess baggage doesn’t include water, it’s a lot lighter. That opens the door for more minimalist solutions like race belts or bib pockets. And once I make this bike my own, I’ll be sewing (or ordering) bags for it. And I won’t need both bottles during the cool, wet times of year, so there’s potential to repurpose one bottle mount for extra layers or food. It is an adventure bike, after all.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Ride Impressions: Descending

And I think Salsa’s adventurous reputation has made it hard for the Blackthorn to get its messages across. Even though Salsa has always made “normal” bikes built for good ol’ Type-1 fun, its name is rarely listed alongside overtly adrenaline-focused brands like Norco or YT or Santa Cruz. That’s why the Blackthorn 125 surprised me so much. It rips.

Like most bikes with this combination of travel and geometry, the Blackthorn 125 keeps you on your toes while also giving you something sturdy to hold onto. But it elevates both of those traits beyond similar bikes. The sturdy thing you can hold onto is its geometry. Most notably, its uniquely long front-center. When I would charge full speed into a section that I absolutely knew would knock me around, there was an imaginary safety net exerting a gentle, calming force that kept me in line. It does nothing to damp the impacts that would be much more manageable with an extra 20 mm of travel. But it makes it so those impacts don’t matter so much.

This of course comes with a long reach measurement. If, like me, you use reach as your north star when picking a bike size, please resist the urge to size down. The seat angle is steep, so your cockpit should feel fine. But more importantly, you’ll have that extended runway when you’re at the blurry edge of this bike’s capability. If anything, look for a handlebar with more backsweep and / or a shorter stem. Maybe even browse our ultra-short high-rise stem listicle, which is also a great way to mitigate the bike’s low stack height

I can’t stress enough how much of a difference my absurdly high cockpit made. It further relieved the stress of those hard front-end hits because I could ride more through my feet and less through my palms. Speaking of my palms, I’ll restate that I’d have preferred stronger brakes with a lighter touch. But that’s an upgrade you can kick down the road. A higher cockpit is more important. It also made for a little more neutral front / rear weight bias, which complemented the Blackthorn 125’s natural flickability. It takes very little effort to briefly slide the back end out to line up for a turn or snake around a rock. That sentence appears in some form every time I review a bike like this, but it especially suits the Blackthorn 125.

One reason is that the frame is quite laterally stiff. That’s no surprise because the chassis was designed to accommodate an extra 20 mm of front and rear travel, along with the extra abuse that invites. There’s also that short chainstay. It provided a good sense of when and where the rear wheel would deflect if I broke traction, intentionally or otherwise. And it made it easier to get the front wheel off the ground for a quick manual or to initiate hopping over an obstacle. I vividly remember two scenarios where I came around a corner to find a freshly fallen wet branch laying diagonally in the trail. The Salsa Blackthorn 125’s slight twitchyness made those quick pop-overs more reflexive.

It also presented some extra challenge when I wanted to make it swiftly but safely to the bottom of the hill. And I mean that in a good way. The firm suspension and short chainstays demand a more hands-on approach in technical sections. This eased off a bit when I swapped to the Linear XL Air Can, which allowed me to access more of the travel more easily, And it of course didn’t compromise the have-fun-but-be-safe geometry. I’m sure a coil shock would take that even a step further. But I’m not sure which configuration I like better. The stock low-volume air setup certainly suited the bike’s playful character.

The Salsa Blackthorn 125’s rear end is not a rudder that you can sink into a wave and coast back to shore. It rewards precision. I guess an XC bike also rewards precision, and is also a challenge. But there’s an important distinction: The source of an XC bike’s challenge is concentrated in front of the bottom bracket, in its short front-center and low handlebars. The Blackthorn 125 (once you’ve fixed its stack height) puts it behind it, with firm suspension and short chainstays. I find that’s a lot safer. The shift from caution to panic is a lot less steep and sudden this way. But there’s still tension. Tension can be fun. It makes a descent more exhilarating and more rewarding. Nothing harsh about that.

Pros:

  • Capable geometry
  • Peppy suspension
    • The traits listed above are in perfect synergy
  • Two in-triangle bottle cages
  • Multiple storage options
  • Smart cable routing
  • Coil compatible
  • Stiffness and durability of a longer-travel frame
  • Can be converted to a longer-travel frame
  • Aluminum option available

Cons:

  • Rear suspension is less plush than some bikes in the already-not-very-plush 125mm category
  • Stack height should be higher
  • Short chainstays aren’t for everyone
